title: Indifference
hookLine: not preferring health to sickness or long life to short, only what leads to God

lines: I DON'T PREFER HEALTH TO SICKNESS?
cards: I don't prefer health to sickness. Say that out loud and it sounds wrong. Yet a sentence like it sits near the very start of the Spiritual Exercises, right after yesterday's foundation.

Ignatius of Loyola writes that a person should not want health more than sickness, riches more than poverty, honor more than dishonor, a long life more than a short one. Read fast, it sounds cold, even alarming.
Read slowly, it's asking for something else. And his word for it does not mean what it means at a dinner party.

teach.b: In ordinary English, indifference is a shrug: whatever, I don't care. Ignatius means nearly the opposite.
Go back to yesterday: we are made to praise, reverence and serve God, and the other things on earth are made to help us toward that end. Then comes the hinge.

teach.h: USE THINGS AS FAR AS THEY HELP.
teach.b: Use things as far as they help, and let them go as far as they hinder.

teach.h: WHERE OUR FREE CHOICE IS ALLOWED.
teach.b: To do that, he says, we have to make ourselves indifferent to all created things, wherever our free choice is allowed. Notice that last part. He isn't telling anyone to skip their medicine or turn down every raise.
Where the choice isn't free, there is nothing to weigh. Where it is free, indifference keeps the scale level until you can see which way leads toward God. Then you choose, with your whole self.
So this is not a lack of feeling.
It's balance before a decision. A person can want health very badly and still hold that wanting open.
Saint Paul says something close in his letter to the Philippians, in the Douay-Rheims: "I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, to be content therewith." Learned. It took practice.
Ignatius ends his sentence with the point: desiring and choosing only what leads more to the end for which we are made.
Because the word can sound like numbness, some teachers reach for others: freedom, availability, open hands. Indifference doesn't make feelings vanish.
It lets them speak, then asks one more question: which of these helps me love God and the people in front of me?

how: In Ignatian retreats, people pray for this inner freedom, which Ignatius calls indifference, before making a major decision, often with the help of a spiritual director.

o: a calm that comes from never making choices
not caring what happens to you at all
a balance that holds choices open before God

games.q: indifference, Ignatius's way — tap the pairs.
p: used as far as they help

s: it's balance before a choice, so you can choose what leads more to God.
Ignatius applies it wherever our free choice is allowed
where there's no free choice, there's nothing to weigh.
indifference means pretending you have no feelings
the feelings can speak. indifference keeps the choice open until the way is clear.

games.q: you're offered a better job in another city, and you want it badly. on Ignatius's terms, what comes first?
o: take it: wanting it is the sign.
refuse it: wanting it is the danger.
hold it open, and ask which way leads toward God.
games.why: the Exercises ask for balance first, then a whole-hearted choice. the wanting isn't wrong; it just isn't the only thing weighed.

practice: Bring to mind one thing you want right now, a real one but not a huge one, and rest your hands open on your knees. Name it silently, I'd like this, then add: and if it goes the other way, I can still walk toward what matters.
If you pray, offer the preference to God for the length of this sit.

wordCard.voice: Indifference. In Ignatius's sense, not a shrug but a balance: holding created things open until you can see which way leads to God. Today's word.

orig.note: Spanish, the language Ignatius wrote the Exercises in: indifferent, balanced, not yet leaning either way.

carryVoice: Your line: hold it loosely. Not a shrug, but open hands before a choice. See you tomorrow.

sources.q: I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, to be content therewith.
